316.title: The Komagata Maru, 1914
316.hook: a ship of mostly Sikh passengers is turned away at Vancouver and returns to violence in India
316.howItsDone: Sikhs in Canada remember the Komagata Maru each year, with Ardas and gatherings at the Vancouver memorial, and tell the story to their children as part of the community's history.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Stockton: the Guru's door, and your line, a door in a new land. Today, a door that stayed shut, and a ship that waited in front of it for two months.

May 1914. A Japanese steamship sails into Vancouver harbor, its rails lined with men in turbans, looking at the city. Three hundred seventy-six passengers, most of them Sikh, all of them British subjects of the same empire as Canada. They've come to work, like the mill men before them. The ship drops anchor. Then nothing happens. Nobody is allowed off. Days pass, then weeks, and the city watches from the shore.
screen: `MAY 1914, VANCOUVER HARBOR.` → `376 PASSENGERS, MOSTLY SIKH.` → `NOBODY IS ALLOWED OFF.`

segments.voice: Remember the rule that closed Canada's door: immigrants had to arrive by a continuous journey from home, and no ships ran straight from India. A Sikh businessman named Gurdit Singh decided to test it. He chartered a ship, the Komagata Maru, filled it with passengers from Punjab, and gave it a new name: Guru Nanak Jahaz, the Guru Nanak ship. At Vancouver, the authorities refused to let the passengers land. The ship sat in the harbor for two months, and food and water ran low. Vancouver's Sikhs, those mill workers, raised money to help and fought in the courts. They lost. Only about twenty passengers, mostly returning residents, were allowed in. In July, with a navy ship standing by, the Komagata Maru was forced to sail away. When it reached India, near Calcutta, in September 1914, British police met it. The passengers were ordered onto a train to Punjab; many refused. There was a confrontation, shots were fired, and around twenty passengers were killed. Others were imprisoned. For decades, Sikhs in Canada kept the memory alive with plaques, books, and a memorial on the Vancouver waterfront, near where the ship once waited. In 2016, Canada's Prime Minister stood in the House of Commons and apologized. It matters because they were turned away not for anything they did, but for who they were and where they were from.

317.title: Bhagat Singh Thind, 1923
317.hook: a Sikh army veteran is denied US citizenship by the Supreme Court
317.howItsDone: Sikh Americans remember Bhagat Singh Thind as a veteran and teacher, and his case is often taught in American history and civil-rights classes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Komagata Maru: two months in Vancouver harbor, and your line, they were turned away. Today, a man who made it in, served, and was still told he didn't belong.

There's an old photograph of a young man in a United States Army uniform from the First World War. Stiff collar, straight back, and on his head, a turban. His name is Bhagat Singh Thind. He came from Punjab to study and worked in lumber mills in Oregon to pay for college. When America went to war, he enlisted, served, and was honorably discharged. Then he applied to become a citizen of the country he'd served, and his case went all the way to the Supreme Court.
screen: `A TURBAN AND AN ARMY UNIFORM.` → `MILLS, COLLEGE, THE WAR.` → `ALL THE WAY TO THE SUPREME COURT.`

segments.voice: At the time, American law let only certain people become citizens by naturalization, and the key words were white persons. Thind was granted citizenship after the war, and the government fought it. His lawyers argued that, by the science of the day, people from north India were counted in the same broad family as Europeans. In February 1923, all nine justices ruled against him. Whatever the scientists said, they held, in the common understanding of ordinary people he was not white, and so could not be a citizen. The ruling hit hard. Other Indian Americans had their citizenship taken away. Some lost land they had bought, because non-citizens couldn't own it in California. Families who had built lives were told, in effect, you're guests here, not members. Thind stayed. He kept teaching and writing, lecturing across America about the spiritual teachings of the Gurus and about finding the divine within. A 1935 law opened citizenship to veterans of the First World War, and in 1936, in New York, he finally became a citizen. It took ten more years before Indians in general could. Now, his name. Bhagat means a devotee. Singh, lion, the name given to Sikh men with the Khalsa. A devoted lion, patient, and stubborn in the good way. The court said he didn't belong. His life said otherwise.

318.title: Britain after 1947
318.hook: Sikhs settle in Southall, Birmingham and the mill towns, building gurdwaras in old houses
318.howItsDone: In Britain, many gurdwaras began in terraced houses, and later in converted churches, cinemas and factories; each morning the Guru Granth Sahib is opened (parkash) and each night it is laid to rest.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhagat: a veteran told he couldn't be a citizen, who stayed, taught, and became one. Your line was he belonged. Today, across the Atlantic, to a gray, rainy Britain after the war.

A row of narrow brick houses in an English town, the 1960s. Every house the same: a front door, a bay window, a little back yard. But on a Sunday morning, one of them is different. Shoes are piled by the front step. Men with covered heads and women in bright scarves go in and out. Through the window comes singing and the beat of a tabla, and from the back, the smell of dal and rotis cooking for everyone who comes.
screen: `A ROW OF BRICK HOUSES.` → `SHOES PILED BY ONE FRONT STEP.` → `SINGING, AND LANGAR COOKING.`

segments.voice: After the Second World War, Britain was short of workers; its factories, foundries and mills needed hands. And after Partition, many Punjabi families had lost land and needed a new start. So from the 1950s Sikh men came, often one from a village first, then his brothers and cousins. They worked in the foundries of Birmingham and the West Midlands, the textile mills of Yorkshire and Lancashire, and the factories and airport near Southall in west London. They shared crowded houses to save money. In the 1960s, wives and children joined them; later, more Sikh families came from Kenya and Uganda. London had had a gurdwara since before the First World War, but most of these new towns had nothing. So Sikhs did what they had done in Hong Kong and California: they bought an ordinary house. The front room, sometimes knocked through into the next, became the darbar: the Guru Granth Sahib on a raised seat under a canopy, the sangat on the carpet before it. The kitchen made langar. Every morning someone performed the parkash, opening the Guru for the day, and every evening laid it to rest. A house became a gurdwara. As the community grew, they bought old churches, cinemas and factories, and eventually built large gurdwaras of their own. But many British Sikh families still talk about that first house: the shoes on the step, the carpet in the front room, langar from a terraced kitchen.

319.title: The turban in court
319.hook: Sikh families win cases in several countries to wear the turban at school and work
319.howItsDone: Many Sikhs keep uncut hair (kesh) and wear a turban (dastar) every day, and Sikh organizations help families and workers who are asked to remove it at school or work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, parkash: foundries, mill towns, and your line, a house became a gurdwara. Today, from one of those British towns, a schoolboy's turban goes all the way to the highest court in the land.

Birmingham, the late 1970s. A father takes his son to a private school to enroll him. The boy is a Sikh, with uncut hair tied up under a small turban. The headmaster is polite, and firm: the boy can come, but the turban must go, and the hair must be cut, to match the school uniform. The father says no. That could have been the end of it: find another school, move on. Instead, the family went to court.
screen: `BIRMINGHAM, THE LATE 1970S.` → `THE TURBAN MUST GO.` → `THE FATHER SAYS NO.`

segments.voice: Why it matters: for many Sikhs, uncut hair, kesh, is a gift to be kept as God made it, and the turban, the dastar, covers and honors it. It is not a hat you take off to be polite. Sikh tradition says Guru Gobind Singh made uncut hair one of the marks of the Khalsa, and for many Sikhs, being told to remove the turban in public is like being told to set aside part of who they are. The boy was Gurinder Singh Mandla. His family lost in the first courts: the appeal judges said Sikhs were a religious group, not a racial one, so the race discrimination law didn't cover them. The family kept going. In 1983 the House of Lords, then Britain's highest court, ruled for them. Sikhs, it said, are a community with a long shared history and culture of their own, an ethnic group under the law, and the school had discriminated. Lawyers still use the test the Lords set out. The question came up beyond the courtroom too. In Britain, Sikh bus drivers campaigned to wear the turban on the job, and won. In Canada, the national police changed its rules in 1990, and Baltej Singh Dhillon joined wearing a turban; later court challenges to the change failed. In the United States, after lawsuits and long campaigns, the Army now lets Sikh soldiers serve with turbans and beards. Each time, a family or a single person said: I can do this job, and learn in this school, and still be myself.

320.title: After September 2001
320.hook: Balbir Singh Sodhi, a Sikh gas station owner in Arizona, is killed in a hate crime
320.howItsDone: Sikh Americans remember Balbir Singh Sodhi each September, and many Sikh organizations run school talks, open gurdwara days and langar for neighbors so people come to know one another.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dastar: a schoolboy in Birmingham, a police officer in Canada, and your line, the right to be yourself. Today, what happened to that right in America in the days after a national tragedy. Go gently.

Mesa, Arizona. Saturday, September fifteenth, 2001, four days after the attacks of September eleventh. The whole country is grieving and afraid. Outside his gas station, a man named Balbir Singh Sodhi is helping a landscaper plant flowers around the sign. Earlier that week, he'd donated to a fund for the victims. He wears a turban and a beard, as many Sikh men do. A pickup truck pulls in.

The man in the truck shot and killed Balbir Singh Sodhi. That same day he fired at other people he thought looked like the enemy, including a Lebanese American clerk and the home of an Afghan American family. When he was arrested, he said he was standing up for America. He was convicted of murder. Balbir Singh Sodhi is remembered as one of the first people killed in a hate crime after September eleventh. He had come to America from Punjab, driven a taxi, saved money with his brothers, and bought that gas station. In the months and years that followed, many Sikhs in America were attacked, insulted or treated with suspicion, most often because of the turban and beard. Now the hard and important part. It would be easy to say: this was a mistake, he wasn't Muslim. Many Sikhs, and many Sikh organizations, refuse to put it that way. The problem, they say, is not who the attacker got wrong. It's attacking anyone because of how they look or what they believe. No one deserves that, Muslim, Sikh or anyone else. That teaching is as old as Guru Nanak, who saw the one light in every person. The Sodhi family answered in the same spirit. Balbir's brother Rana spent years speaking in schools, churches and community halls, telling his brother's story so people would know their Sikh neighbors. Ignorance was the soil. Knowing each other is the cure.

321.title: Oak Creek, 2012
321.hook: six worshipers are killed at a Wisconsin gurdwara, and the sangat answers with prayer and open doors
321.howItsDone: Each August the Oak Creek sangat remembers those killed with Ardas, kirtan and a community run named for chardi kala, and the gurdwara continues to welcome neighbors to langar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, guandhi: Balbir Singh Sodhi, and a brother who told his story. Your line was know your neighbor. Today, another hard day, and an answer that drew strangers in. Go gently.

A Sunday morning in August, in Oak Creek, a suburb near Milwaukee, Wisconsin. At the gurdwara, women are in the kitchen getting langar ready for the Sunday crowd. A few people already sit with the Guru Granth Sahib; more families are on their way. An ordinary Sunday. Then a man walks in from the parking lot with a gun.
screen: `A SUNDAY IN AUGUST, WISCONSIN.` → `LANGAR BEING READIED.` → `A MAN FROM THE PARKING LOT.`

segments.voice: On August 5, 2012, a gunman who held white supremacist views killed six people at the Sikh Temple of Wisconsin. The gurdwara's president, Satwant Singh Kaleka, tried to stop him and was killed. So were Paramjit Kaur, Prakash Singh, Sita Singh, Ranjit Singh and Suveg Singh. They had names. A granthi, Baba Punjab Singh, was badly wounded and died of his injuries years later. A police officer, Lieutenant Brian Murphy, was shot many times helping, and survived. The gunman killed himself. Then the sangat held Ardas for the dead. When the police handed the building back, they cleaned the hall and opened the doors. For weeks after, they welcomed neighbors, reporters, police officers and strangers, and fed them langar. Some had never been inside a gurdwara, and were handed a plate by the people who had just been attacked. Since then, the community has marked the anniversary with a remembrance run named for chardi kala, rising spirits. Satwant Singh Kaleka's son, Pardeep, later became friends with a man who had once been a white supremacist himself, and together they went into schools to talk about hate and how people leave it. It hasn't ended: in recent years Sikhs in several countries, the US and Britain among them, have still been attacked for how they look. If it ever happens to you or someone near you, get safe first, and call emergency help if anyone's in danger. Then tell someone, and report it; in the US, the Sikh Coalition helps. The grief was not small. But in Sikh teaching, the sangat, the holy company, is where the Guru is found. When it was hurt, it stayed together, and it stayed open.

322.title: Langar where disaster strikes
322.hook: Sikh volunteers cook free meals after floods, earthquakes and wars around the world
322.howItsDone: Gurdwaras serve free langar to anyone every day, and Sikh volunteers and aid groups set up kitchens after disasters and at refugee crossings, as seva, selfless service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Oak Creek: six worshipers killed, and a sangat that fed strangers the same week. Your line was the doors stayed open. Today, the kitchen behind those doors goes out into the world.

A border crossing in winter. Thousands of families have just walked out of a war zone, carrying what they could. They're cold, and nobody has eaten properly in days. At the edge of the crowd, under a tent, a few people in turbans and orange scarves are stirring enormous pots: rice, dal, hot tea with milk and sugar. Anyone can take a plate. No one asks your name, your religion or your papers. Scenes like this have turned up after floods, earthquakes and wars.
screen: `A BORDER CROSSING IN WINTER.` → `ENORMOUS POTS UNDER A TENT.` → `NO ONE ASKS YOUR NAME.`

segments.voice: Langar has been on this path from the start: the gurdwara's free kitchen, where everyone sits on the same floor and eats the same food. At the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, the kitchen runs all day for whoever comes. Sikhs trace it to Guru Nanak. A janamsakhi story says that when Nanak was a young man, his father gave him money to strike a good bargain, and he spent it all feeding hungry holy men on the road. He called it the true bargain. Guru Angad and his wife, Mata Khivi, built the kitchen into daily life, and tradition says Guru Amar Das asked visitors to eat in the langar before they met him, rich or poor, side by side. Now the langar travels. In 1999, a British Sikh started Khalsa Aid by taking food and supplies to refugees from the war in Kosovo. Since then, Sikh volunteers, from that group and many others, have cooked for flood victims, earthquake survivors, refugees at borders, protesters, and people locked down in the pandemic. In Houston after a hurricane, local Sikhs loaded their cars with hot meals. In their own cities, gurdwaras have fed truck drivers stuck on the highway and neighbors who lost power. Why? Seva, selfless service, and the teaching that the one light is in everyone. The hungry person at a border is not a stranger to be pitied, but a guest at the Guru's table. This week ran from the Komagata Maru, Thind, Britain, the turban in court, September 2001 and Oak Creek to this: langar going out to the world.
screen: `LANGAR: THE GURU'S KITCHEN.` · `THE TRUE BARGAIN.` · `FOOD AT BORDERS, FLOODS, QUAKES.` · `A GUEST AT THE GURU'S TABLE.` · then, large: `THE KITCHEN TRAVELS.`

segments.voice: Think of a place where people are hungry or displaced right now, after a flood, a quake or a war, and picture one family there sitting down to a plate of warm food someone else cooked. Let yourself feel glad for that plate. Then choose one way you could help, however small: a donation, a volunteer hour, a meal for a neighbor.
Langar. The gurdwara's free kitchen — Sikh volunteers carry it to disaster, cooking free meals for anyone after floods, earthquakes and wars around the world.
Your line: the kitchen travels. From Kosovo to Houston, the pots keep stirring. That's day three hundred twenty-two.
